newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean central bank sees growth slowing.
newsitem.headline: South Korean central bank sees growth slowing.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Friday lowered its projection for economic growth this year and predicted inflation would edge higher, adding to a slew of gloomy statistics on the economy.
Nevertheless, assistant bank governor Kim Young-dae said the economy may pick up in the second half of this year as the benefits of an austerity programme began to show.
Just two weeks ago, Kim said there was no possibility of a rebound this year.

The bank said in a statement on Friday it was revising its forecast for gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 to a real 5.5 percent to 6.0 percent from 6.4 percent. Growth last year was 7.1 percent.
The consumer price index, a leading indicator of inflation, was expected to grow by 4.7 percent this year against a 4.5 percent rise in 1996, the bank said.
It said the current account deficit could exceed a previously forecast $18 billion in 1997. The deficit reached $23.72 billion last year.
"A downward revision on economic growth is inevitable as the government is pushing ahead with austerity steps aimed at cutting the current account deficit and fighting inflation," Kim said.
"Pain will follow, but recovery will come earlier," he said. "The economy can possibly pick up from the second half of this year.
Last month Kim predicted 1997 growth at 6.0 percent and said chances of an upturn this year had fizzled.
On Friday he said he had changed his mind on optimism that the government would not try any quick-fix economic solutions.

The government has said it will slash two trillion won ($2.2 billion) from its budget spending this year and lower tax revenue by an equivalent amount to reduce demand and bring down the current account deficit.
Finance minister Kang Kyong-shik on Thursday warned the economy was in "serious trouble" but he ruled out any fiscal stimulus measures to revive it.
The current account deficit has been fuelled by plunging prices for exports, particularly semiconductors.
"Exports are likely to improve towards the end of this year with a recovery in export prices, but imports would continue to slow due to falling consumption and investment," Kim said.
The spot price for 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips rebounded to $10-$11 per unit in March from $6-$7 in January and February. This compares with $40-$50 at the end of 1995.
"A one dollar rise in the prices of semiconductors is calculated to cut the current account deficit by $800 million," Kim said.
Inflation is being fuelled by a falling won, which is pushing up the price of imports. The won has fallen by about six percent against the dollar this year.

On Thursday the Bank of Korea said M2 money supply -- including money in circulation and bank savings and checking accounts -- rose 20.5 percent in March year-on-year compared with a 14.6 percent increase a year earlier.
Unemployment rose to a three-year high of 3.2 percent in February.
